{{Short description|Well studied projective geometries over finite fields}}
A frequently studied problem in [[finite geometry]] is to identify ways in which an object can be covered by other simpler objects such as points, lines, and planes. In [[projective geometry]], a specific instance of this problem that has numerous applications is determining whether, and how, a projective space can be covered by pairwise disjoint subspaces which have the same dimension; such a partition is called a '''spread'''. Specifically, a '''spread''' of a projective space [[Projective geometry|<math>PG(d,K)</math>]], where <math>d \geq 1</math> is an [[integer]] and <math>K</math> a [[division ring]], is a set of <math>r</math>-dimensional subspaces, for some <math>0 < r < d</math> such that every point of the space lies in exactly one of the elements of the spread.

Spreads are particularly well-studied in projective geometries over finite fields, though some notable results apply to infinite projective geometries as well. In the finite case, the foundational work on spreads appears in André<ref name=":0">{{Citation | last1=André | first1=Johannes | title=Über nicht-Desarguessche Ebenen mit transitiver Translationsgruppe | url=http://resolver.sub.uni-goettingen.de/purl?GDZPPN002384345 | doi=10.1007/BF01187370 | mr=0063056 | year=1954 | journal=[[Mathematische Zeitschrift]] | issn=0025-5874 | volume=60 | pages=156–186| s2cid=123661471 | url-access=subscription }}</ref> and independently in Bruck-Bose<ref name=BB>{{citation| last1 =Bruck  | first1 = R. H. | author1-link = Richard Bruck|first2=R. C.|last2= Bose   | title = The Construction of Translation Planes from Projective Spaces  | journal= Journal of Algebra|volume=1| year =1964  | pages = 85–102 | doi=10.1016/0021-8693(64)90010-9| url = http://repository.lib.ncsu.edu/bitstream/1840.4/2172/1/ISMS_1963_378.pdf}}</ref> in connection with the theory of [[translation plane]]s. In these papers, it is shown that a spread of <math>r</math>-dimensional subspaces of the finite projective space <math>PG(d,q)</math> exists if and only if <math> r+1 \mid d+1</math>.<ref>This is ultimately a consequence of the fact that a [[Finite field#Existence and uniqueness|finite field]] of order <math>p^{d+1}</math> has a subfield of order <math>p^{r+1}</math> if and only if <math> r+1 \mid d+1</math>.</ref>

==Spreads and translation planes==
For all integers <math>n \geq 1</math>, the projective space <math>PG(2n+1,q)</math> always has a spread of <math>n</math>-dimensional subspaces, and in this section the term '''spread''' refers to this specific type of spread; spreads of this form may (and frequently do) occur in infinite projective geometries as well. These spreads are the most widely studied in the literature, due to the fact that every such spread can be used to create a [[translation plane]] using the André/Bruck-Bose construction.<ref name=":0"/><ref name=BB/>
===Reguli and regular spreads===
Let <math>\Sigma</math> be the [[Projective geometry|projective space]] <math>PG(2n+1,K)</math> for <math>n \geq 1</math> an integer, and <math>K</math> a division ring. A ''[[regulus (geometry)|regulus]]''<ref>This notion generalizes that of a classical regulus, which is one of the two families of ruling lines on a [[hyperboloid of one sheet]] in 3-dimensional space</ref> <math>R</math> in <math>\Sigma</math> is a collection of pairwise disjoint <math>n</math>-dimensional subspaces with the following properties:
# <math>R</math> contains at least 3 elements
# Every line meeting three elements of <math>R</math>, called a ''[[Transversal (combinatorics)|transversal]]'', meets every element of <math>R</math>
# Every point of a transversal to <math>R</math> lies on some element of <math>R</math>

Any three pairwise disjoint <math>n</math>-dimensional subspaces in <math>\Sigma</math> lie in a unique regulus.<ref>{{citation| last1 =Bruck  | first1 = R. H. | author1-link = Richard Bruck|first2=R. C.|last2= Bose   | title = Linear Representations of Projective Planes in Projective Spaces  | journal= Journal of Algebra|volume=4| year =1966  | pages = 117–172 | doi=10.1016/0021-8693(66)90054-8| url = https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0021869366900548/pdf?md5=5da6e196f623be3d1ddbe488da202e43&pid=1-s2.0-0021869366900548-main.pdf}}, page 163</ref> A spread <math>S</math> of <math>\Sigma</math> is ''regular'' if for any three distinct <math>n</math>-dimensional subspaces of <math>S</math>, all the members of the unique regulus determined by them are contained in <math>S</math>. Regular spreads are significant in the theory of [[translation plane]]s, in that they generate [[Moufang plane]]s in general, and [[Desarguesian plane]]s in the finite case when the order of the ambient field is greater than <math>2</math>. All spreads of <math>PG(2n+1,2)</math> are trivially regular, since a regulus only contains three elements.

===Constructing a regular spread===

Construction of a regular spread is most easily seen using an algebraic model. Letting <math>V</math> be a <math>(2n+2)</math>-dimensional [[vector space]] over a [[Field (mathematics)|field]] <math>F</math>, one can model the <math>k</math>-dimensional subspaces of <math>PG(2n+1,F)</math> using the <math>(k+1)</math>-dimensional subspaces of <math>V</math>; this model uses [[homogeneous coordinates]] to represent points and hyperplanes. Incidence is defined by intersection, with subspaces intersecting in only the zero vector considered disjoint; in this model, the zero vector of <math>V</math> is effectively ignored.

Let <math>F</math> be a field and <math>E</math> an <math>n</math>-dimensional [[extension field]] of <math>F</math>. Consider <math>V = E \oplus E</math> as a <math>2n</math>-dimensional vector space over <math>F</math>, which provides a model for the projective space <math>PG(2n-1,F)</math> as above. Each element of <math>V</math> can be written uniquely as <math>(x,y)</math> where <math>x,y \in E</math>. A regular spread is given by the set of <math>n</math>-dimensional projective spaces defined by <math>J(k) = \{(x,kx):x \in E\}</math>, for each <math>k \in E</math>, together with <math>J(\infty) = \{(0,y):y \in E\}</math>.<ref name=EM>{{citation|url=http://www.uwyo.edu/moorhouse/handouts/incidence_geometry.pdf|title=Incidence Geometry|year=2007|first=Eric|last=Moorhouse|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131029221809/http://www.uwyo.edu/moorhouse/handouts/incidence_geometry.pdf|archivedate=2013-10-29}}</ref>

== Constructing spreads ==
=== Spread sets ===
The construction of a regular spread above is an instance of a more general construction of spreads, which uses the fact that field multiplication is a [[linear map|linear transformation]] over <math>E</math> when considered as a vector space. Since <math>E</math> is a finite <math>n</math>-dimensional extension over <math>F</math>, a linear transformation from <math>E</math> to itself can be represented by an <math>n \times n</math> matrix with entries in <math>F</math>. A ''spread set'' is a set <math>S</math> of <math>n \times n</math> matrices over <math>F</math> with the following properties:
* <math>S</math> contains the [[zero matrix]] and the identity matrix
* For any two distinct matrices <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> in <math>S</math>, <math>X-Y</math> is nonsingular
* For each pair of elements <math>a,b \in E</math>, there is a unique <math>X \in S</math> such that <math>aX = b</math>

In the finite case, where <math>E</math> is the field of order <math>q^n</math> for some prime power <math>q</math>, the last condition is equivalent to the spread set containing <math>q^n</math> matrices. Given a spread set <math>S</math>, one can create a spread as the set of <math>n</math>-dimensional projective spaces defined by <math>J(k) = \{(x,xM):x \in E\}</math>, for each <math>M \in S</math>, together with <math>J(\infty) = \{(0,y):y \in E\}</math>,<ref name=BB/>
As a specific example, the following nine matrices represent <math>GF(9)</math> as 2 × 2 matrices over <math>GF(3)</math> and so provide a spread set of <math>AG(2, 9)</math>.<ref name=EM/>
:<math> \left [ \begin{matrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{matrix} \right ], \left [ \begin{matrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{matrix} \right ], \left [ \begin{matrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{matrix} \right ], \left [ \begin{matrix} 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 \end{matrix} \right ], \left [ \begin{matrix} 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{matrix} \right ], \left [ \begin{matrix} 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 \end{matrix} \right ], \left [ \begin{matrix} 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \end{matrix} \right ], \left [ \begin{matrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{matrix} \right ], \left [ \begin{matrix} 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{matrix} \right ]</math>

Another example of a spread set yields the [[Hall plane#The Hall plane of order 9|Hall plane of order 9]]<ref name=EM/>
:<math> \left [ \begin{matrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{matrix} \right ], \left [ \begin{matrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{matrix} \right ], \left [ \begin{matrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{matrix} \right ], \left [ \begin{matrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{matrix} \right ], \left [ \begin{matrix} 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{matrix} \right ], \left [ \begin{matrix} 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 \end{matrix} \right ], \left [ \begin{matrix} 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \end{matrix} \right ], \left [ \begin{matrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{matrix} \right ], \left [ \begin{matrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{matrix} \right ]</math>

===Modifying spreads===
One common approach to creating new spreads is to start with a regular spread and modify it in some way. The techniques presented here are some of the more elementary examples of this approach.

====Spreads of 3-space====
One can create new spreads by starting with a spread and looking for a ''switching set'', a subset of its elements that can be replaced with an alternate set of pairwise disjoint 
subspaces of the correct dimension. In <math>PG(3,K)</math>, a [[regulus]] forms a switching set, as the set of transversals of a regulus <math>R</math> also form a regulus, called the ''opposite regulus'' of <math>R</math>. Removing the lines of a regulus in a spread and replacing them with the opposite regulus produces a new spread which is often non-isomorphic to the original. This process is a special case of a more general process called ''derivation'' or ''net replacement''.<ref>{{citation|first1=Norman L.|last1=Johnson|first2=Vikram|last2=Jha|first3=Mauro|last3=Biliotti|title=Handbook of Finite Translation Planes|year=2007|publisher=Chapman&Hall/CRC|isbn=978-1-58488-605-1}}, page 49</ref>

Starting with a regular spread of <math>PG(3,q)</math> and reversing any regulus produces a spread that yields a [[Hall plane]]. In more generality, the process can be applied independently to any collection of reguli in a regular spread, yielding a ''subregular spread<ref>{{Citation|last=Bruck|first=R.H.|title=Construction Problems of finite projective planes|work=Combinatorial Mathematics and Its Applications|publisher=Univ. of North Carolina Press|year=1969|isbn=|editor-last=R.C.Bose and T.A. Dowling|location=|pages=426–514}}</ref>''; the resulting translation plane is called a [[subregular plane]]. The [[André plane]]s form a special subclass of subregular planes, of which the [[Hall plane]]s are the simplest examples, arising by replacing a single regulus in a regular spread.

More complex switching sets have been constructed. Bruen<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Bruen|first=A.A.|date=1978|title=Inversive geometry and some translation planes, I|url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00181353|journal=Geometriae Dedicata|language=en|volume=7|pages=81–98|doi=10.1007/BF00181353|s2cid=122632353|via=|url-access=subscription}}</ref> has explored the concept of a ''chain'' of reguli in a regular spread of <math>PG(3,q)</math>, <math>q</math> odd, namely a set of <math>(q+3)/2</math> reguli which pairwise meet in exactly 2 lines, so that every line contained in a regulus of the chain is contained in exactly two distinct reguli of the chain. Bruen constructed an example of a chain in the regular spread of <math>PG(3,5)</math>, and showed that it could be replaced by taking the union of exactly half of the lines from the opposite regulus of each regulus in the chain. Numerous examples of Bruen chains have appeared in the literature since, and Heden<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Heden|first=O.|date=1995|title=On Bruen chains|url=https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/82018218.pdf|journal=Discrete Mathematics|language=en|volume=146|issue=1–3|pages=69–96|doi=10.1016/0012-365X(94)00058-0|via=|doi-access=free}}</ref> has shown that any Bruen chain is replaceable using opposite half-reguli. Chains are known to exist in a regular spread of <math>PG(3,q)</math> for all odd prime powers <math>q</math> up to 37, except 29, and are known not to exist for <math>q \in \{29,41,43,47,49\}</math>.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Johnson|first1=Norman L.|title=Handbook of Finite Translation Planes|last2=Jha|first2=Vikram|last3=Biliotti|first3=Mauro|publisher=Chapman & Hall/CRC|year=2007|isbn=978-1-58488-605-1|location=Boca Raton, FL|chapter=Nests}}</ref> It is conjectured that no additional Bruen chains exist.

Baker and Ebert<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Baker|first1=R. D.|last2=Ebert|first2=G. L.|date=1988|title=Nests of size <math>q-1</math> and another family of translation planes|url=https://londmathsoc.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/toc/14697750/1988/s2-38/2|journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society|volume=38|issue=2|pages=341–355|doi=10.1112/jlms/s2-38.2.341|url-access=subscription}}</ref> generalized the concept of a chain to a ''nest'', which is a set of reguli in a regular spread such that every line contained in a regulus of the nest is contained in exactly two distinct reguli of the nest. Unlike a chain, two reguli in a nest are not required to meet in a pair of lines. Unlike chains, a nest in a regular spread need not be replaceable,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ebert|first=G. L.|date=1988|title=Some nonreplaceable nests|journal=Combinatorics '88|volume=1|publisher=Research Lecture Notes in Mathematics, Mediterranean, Rende|pages=353–372}}</ref> however several infinite families of replaceable nests are known.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Baker|first1=R. D.|last2=Ebert|first2=G. L.|date=1988|title=A new class of translation planes|journal=Annals of Discrete Mathematics|location=Amsterdam|publisher=North-Holland|volume=37|pages=7–20|doi=10.1016/S0167-5060(08)70220-6|isbn=9780444703699}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Baker|first1=R. D.|last2=Ebert|first2=G. L.|date=1996|title=Filling the nest gaps|journal=Finite Fields and Applications|volume=2|issue=1|pages=45–61}}</ref>

====Higher-dimensional spreads====
In higher dimensions a regulus cannot be reversed because the transversals do not have the correct dimension. There exist analogs to reguli, called ''norm surfaces'', which can be reversed.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Bruck|first=R.H.|date=1973|title=Circle geometry in higher dimensions. II|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF00147854|journal=Geometriae Dedicata|language=en|volume=2|issue=2|pages=|doi=10.1007/BF00147854|s2cid=189889878|issn=0046-5755|via=|url-access=subscription}}</ref> The higher-dimensional [[André plane]]s can be obtained from spreads obtained by reversing these norm surfaces, and there also exist analogs of subregular spreads which do not give rise to [[André plane]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Dover|first=Jeremy|date=1998|title=Subregular Spreads of PG(2n+1,q)|journal=Finite Fields and Their Applications|language=en|volume=4|issue=4|pages=362–380|doi=10.1006/ffta.1998.0222|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Culbert|first1=Craig|last2=Ebert|first2=Gary|date=2005|title=Circle geometry and three-dimensional subregular translation planes|url=https://msp.org/iig/2005/1-1/p01.xhtml|journal=Innovations in Incidence Geometry: Algebraic, Topological and Combinatorial|language=en|volume=1|issue=1|pages=3–18|doi=10.2140/iig.2005.1.3|issn=1781-6475|doi-access=free}}</ref>

===Geometric techniques===
There are several known ways to construct spreads of <math>PG(3,q)</math> from other geometrical objects without reference to an initial regular spread. Some well-studied approaches to this are given below.

====Flocks of quadratic cones====
In <math>PG(3,q)</math>, a ''quadratic cone'' is the union of the set of lines containing a fixed point P (the ''vertex'') and a point on a [[Conic section|conic]] in a plane not passing through P. Since a conic has <math>q+1</math> points, a quadratic cone has <math>q(q+1)+1</math> points. As with traditional geometric [[conic section]]s, a plane of <math>PG(3,q)</math> can meet a quadratic cone in either a point, a conic, a line or a line pair. A ''flock'' of a quadratic cone is a set of <math>q</math> planes whose intersections with the quadratic cone are pairwise disjoint conics. The classic construction of a flock is to pick a line <math>m</math> that does not meet the quadratic cone, and take the <math>q</math> planes through <math>m</math> that do not contain the vertex of the cone; such a flock is called ''linear''.

Fisher and Thas<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Fisher|first1=J. Chris|last2=Thas|first2=Joseph A.|date=1979|title=Flocks in PG(3,q)|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF01214908|journal=Mathematische Zeitschrift|language=en|volume=169|issue=1|pages=1–11|doi=10.1007/BF01214908|s2cid=121796426|issn=0025-5874|url-access=subscription}}</ref> show how to construct a spread of <math>PG(3,q)</math> from a flock of a quadratic cone using the [[Klein quadric|Klein correspondence]], and show that the resulting spread is regular [[if and only if]] the initial flock is linear. Many infinite families of flocks of quadratic cones are known, as are numerous sporadic examples.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Johnson|first1=Norman L.|title=Handbook of Finite Translation Planes|last2=Jha|first2=Vikram|last3=Biliotti|first3=Mauro|publisher=Chapman & Hall/CRC|year=2007|isbn=978-1-58488-605-1|location=Boca Raton, FL|chapter=Infinite Classes of Flocks}}</ref>

Every spread arising from a flock of a quadratic cone is the union of <math>q</math> reguli which all meet in a fixed line <math>m</math>. Much like with a regular spread, any of these reguli can be replaced with its opposite to create several potentially new spreads.<ref>A specific example of this phenomenon is illustrated in {{cite arXiv|last=Dover|first=Jeremy M.|date=2019-02-27|title=A genealogy of the translation planes of order 25|class=math.CO|eprint=1902.07838}} to relate two translation planes of order 25 found by computer search in {{Cite journal|last1=Czerwinski|first1=Terry|last2=Oakden|first2=David|date=1992|title=The translation planes of order twenty-five|journal=Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A|language=en|volume=59|issue=2|pages=193–217|doi=10.1016/0097-3165(92)90065-3|doi-access=}}</ref>

====Hyperbolic fibrations====
In <math>PG(3,q)</math> a hyperbolic fibration is a partition of the space into <math>q-1</math> pairwise disjoint hyperbolic quadrics and two lines disjoint from all of the quadrics and each other. Since a hyperbolic quadric consists of the points covered by a regulus and its opposite, a hyperbolic fibration yields <math>2^{q-1}</math> different spreads.

All spreads yielding [[André plane]]s, including the regular spread, are obtainable from a hyperbolic fibration (specifically an [[Pencil (mathematics)|algebraic pencil]] generated by any two of the quadrics), as articulated by André.<ref name=":0" /> Using nest replacement, Ebert<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ebert|first=G. L.|date=1989|title=Spreads Admitting Regular Elliptic Covers|journal=European Journal of Combinatorics|language=en|volume=10|issue=4|pages=319–330|doi=10.1016/S0195-6698(89)80004-6|doi-access=}}</ref> found a family of spreads in which a hyperbolic fibration was identified. Baker, et al.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Baker|first1=R. D.|last2=Dover|first2=J. M.|last3=Ebert|first3=G. L.|last4=Wantz|first4=K. L.|date=1999|title=Hyperbolic Fibrations of PG(3,q)|journal=European Journal of Combinatorics|language=en|volume=20|issue=1|pages=1–16|doi=10.1006/eujc.1998.0249|doi-access=free}}</ref> provide an explicit example of a construction of a hyperbolic fibration. A much more robust source of hyperbolic fibrations was identified by Baker, et al.,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Baker|first1=R. D.|last2=Ebert|first2=G. L.|last3=Penttila|first3=Tim|date=2005|title=Hyperbolic Fibrations and q-Clans|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s10623-004-4861-8|journal=Designs, Codes and Cryptography|language=en|volume=34|issue=2–3|pages=295–305|doi=10.1007/s10623-004-4861-8|s2cid=21853272|issn=0925-1022|url-access=subscription}}</ref> where the authors developed a correspondence between flocks of quadratic cones and hyperbolic fibrations; interestingly, the spreads generated by a flock of a quadratic cone are not generally isomorphic to the spreads generated from the corresponding hyperbolic fibration.

==== Subgeometry partitions ====
Hirschfeld and Thas<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Hirschfeld|first1=J. W. P.|title=General Galois geometries|last2=Thas|first2=J. A.|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=1991|isbn=978-1-4471-6790-7|location=London|pages=206|oclc=936691484}}</ref> note that for any odd integer <math>n \geq 3</math>, a partition of <math>PG(n-1,q^2)</math> into subgeometries isomorphic to <math>PG(n-1,q)</math> gives rise to a spread of <math>PG(2n-1,q)</math>, where each subgeometry of the partition corresponds to a regulus of the new spread.

The "classical" subgeometry partitions of <math>PG(n-1,q^2)</math> can be generated using suborbits of a Singer cycle, but this simply generates a regular spread.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Bruck|first=R. H.|url=http://www.ams.org/psapm/010|title=Combinatorial Analysis|publisher=American Mathematical Society|year=1960|isbn=978-0-8218-1310-2|editor-last=Bellman|editor-first=Richard|series=Proceedings of Symposia in Applied Mathematics|volume=10|location=Providence, Rhode Island|pages=15–44|language=en|chapter=Quadratic extensions of cyclic planes|doi=10.1090/psapm/010|editor-last2=Hall|editor-first2=Marshall}}</ref> Yff<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Yff|first=Peter|date=1977|title=On subplane partitions of a finite projective plane|journal=Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A|language=en|volume=22|issue=1|pages=118–122|doi=10.1016/0097-3165(77)90072-3|doi-access=}}</ref> published the non-classical subgeometry partition, namely a partition of <math>PG(2,9)</math> into 7 copies of <math>PG(2,3)</math>, that admit a [[cyclic group]] permuting the subplanes. Baker, et al.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Baker|first1=Ronald D.|last2=Dover|first2=Jeremy M.|last3=Ebert|first3=Gary L.|last4=Wantz|first4=Kenneth L.|date=2000|title=Baer subgeometry partitions|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF01220294|journal=Journal of Geometry|language=en|volume=67|issue=1–2|pages=23–34|doi=10.1007/BF01220294|s2cid=121116940|issn=0047-2468|url-access=subscription}}</ref> provide several infinite families of partitions of <math>PG(2,q^2)</math> into subplanes, with the same cyclic [[group action]].

== Partial spreads ==
A ''partial spread'' of a [[Projective geometry|projective space]] <math>PG(d,K)</math> is a set of pairwise disjoint <math>r</math>-dimensional subspaces in the space; hence a spread is just a partial spread where every point of the space is covered.  A partial spread is called ''complete'' or ''maximal'' if there is no larger partial spread that contains it; equivalently, there is no <math>r</math>-dimensional subspace disjoint from all members of the partial spread. As with spreads, the most well-studied case is partial spreads of lines of the finite projective space <math>PG(3,q)</math>, where a full spread has size <math>q^2+1</math>. Mesner<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Mesner|first=Dale M.|date=1967|title=Sets of Disjoint Lines in PG(3, q)|journal=Canadian Journal of Mathematics|language=en|volume=19|pages=273–280|doi=10.4153/CJM-1967-019-5|s2cid=123550829 |issn=0008-414X|doi-access=free}}</ref> showed that any partial spread of lines in <math>PG(3,q)</math> with size greater than <math>q^2 - \sqrt{q}</math> cannot be complete; indeed, it must be a subset of a unique spread. For a lower bound, Bruen<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Bruen|first=A.|date=1971|title=Partial Spreads and Replaceable Nets|journal=Canadian Journal of Mathematics|language=en|volume=23|issue=3|pages=381–391|doi=10.4153/CJM-1971-039-x|s2cid=124356288 |issn=0008-414X|doi-access=free}}</ref> showed that a complete partial spread of lines in <math>PG(3,q)</math> with size at most <math>q+\sqrt{q}</math> lines cannot be complete; there will necessarily be a line that can be added to a partial spread of this size. Bruen also provides examples of complete partial spreads of lines in <math>PG(3,q)</math> with sizes <math>q^2-q+1</math> and <math>q^2-q+2</math> for all <math>q > 2</math>.

== Spreads of classical polar spaces ==
The [[Polar space#Finite classical polar spaces|classical polar spaces]] are all embedded in some projective space <math>PG(d,K)</math> as the set of [[Isotropic quadratic form|totally isotropic subspaces]] of a [[Sesquilinear form|sesquilinear]] or [[quadratic form]] on the vector space underlying the projective space. A particularly interesting class of partial spreads of <math>PG(d,K)</math> are those that consist strictly of maximal subspaces of a classical polar space embedded in the projective space. Such partial spreads that cover all of the points of the polar space are called ''spreads'' of the polar space.

From the perspective of the theory of translation planes, the [[Symplectic vector space|symplectic]] polar space is of particular interest, as its set of points are all of the points in <math>PG(2n+1,K)</math>, and its maximal subspaces are of dimension <math>n</math>. Hence a spread of the symplectic polar space is also a spread of the entire projective space, and can be used as noted above to create a translation plane. Several examples of symplectic spreads are known; see Ball, et al.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ball|first1=Simeon|last2=Bamberg|first2=John|last3=Lavrauw|first3=Michel|last4=Penttila|first4=Tim|date=May 2004|title=Symplectic Spreads|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1023/B:DESI.0000029209.24742.89|journal=Designs, Codes and Cryptography|language=en|volume=32|issue=1–3|pages=9–14|doi=10.1023/B:DESI.0000029209.24742.89|s2cid=8228870|issn=0925-1022|url-access=subscription}}</ref>
